Question: As a computer engineer what coding languages should I learn (name them please)?
Old_Answer: Don’t worry about which languages matter when you are starting out. Instead, think of it this way: through your career you will more than likely use lots of languages. I’ve lost count. I know it’s more than 40, though the vast majority of my work has been in only six of those. So the trick is to learn how to learn languages quickly. You do this by learning lots of languages early on. But first, you have to learn programming, which is a language-independent skill. Unfortunately, you have to learn a whole stack of things simultaneously when you start out: programming itself, debugging, some language, and some set of tools that will let you use that language (an editor, maybe a build system, maybe a debugger, version control…) Your first language should probably be something relatively easy, as you have all that extra load to deal with. Easy languages, however, are not typically the really important languages, either important because they’re widely used in industry, or important because of what they teach you. Later, whatever your first language, you should spend a bit of time learning one from each major language family (procedural, functional, object oriented, dynamic, lazily evaluated, declarative, etc). That will make the ones you have to learn later much easier.

Answer_with_full_information: When considering the creation of a transport layer protocol that could outperform TCP and UDP, it's essential to explore both conceptual and practical aspects of network communication. Question: Do multiple people sharing an Internet connection each have their own unique external IP address?
Old_Answer: Most of the time, in IPv4, no. Almost always in IPv6, yes. IPv4 does not have enough addresses to number the current Internet, so addresses are shared, by use of NAT (network address translation, which comes in several varieties). In fact, it’s fairly common that external IP addresses will be shared between multiple connections (so-called Carrier Grade NAT, for example). More than likely you have never used a network that didn’t share IPv4 addresses. IPv6 has plenty of addresses, so while NAT is possible, it’s very rare. Most devices on an IPv6 network will have many addresses, in fact. So… it depends.
Answer_with_writing_sample: No, they don’t. When multiple devices connect to the Internet through the same router, they typically share a single external IP address. Think of it like a household with one mailbox; each person living there has their own internal address (like room numbers), but they all receive mail at that one mailbox. This external IP address is assigned by your Internet Service Provider (ISP) and is how the outside world sees your home network. However, within the home network, each device has its own internal IP address (like IP 192.168.x.x, for example), which allows the router to send data to the correct device. If those multiple connections create a lot of traffic, it could slow your connection down, but they’ll still all operate through that same external address. In essence, you can have a bustling household online without needing multiple mailboxes!
Answer_with_user_profile: When multiple people share an Internet connection, they typically do not each have their own unique external IP address; rather, they usually share a single external IP address. This common scenario occurs because most home and small business networks use a router that employs Network Address Translation (NAT). The router assigns private internal IP addresses to each device connected to the network, and it serves as an intermediary between these devices and the internet. When any of the devices send data to the internet, the router replaces the private IP address with its own external IP address. Consequently, to external servers and websites, it appears as if all traffic comes from a single IP address. This setup is efficient and cost-effective, allowing multiple devices to access the Internet using a single Internet Service Provider (ISP) subscription. However, in certain cases, some advanced ISPs and business networks may provide distinct external IP addresses for multiple devices, especially if configured for dedicated applications or through specialized services. In summary, while the standard arrangement for shared connections is one external IP address for all devices, there are exceptions based on specific networking configurations or services.
Answer_with_full_information: When multiple people share an internet connection, they typically do not each have their own unique external IP address. Instead, the network usually operates under a single public IP address, which is assigned to the router by the Internet Service Provider (ISP). This means that all devices connected to the router are using this single external IP to access the internet. However, within the local network, each device is assigned a unique internal IP address, allowing the router to distinguish between them. This setup is known as Network Address Translation (NAT), and it effectively enables multiple devices to communicate with the outside world while only utilizing one public IP. Think of it like a single postal address for an apartment building: while each tenant (or device) has their own apartment number (internal IP), all of them share the same main entrance (external IP) when receiving mail (internet traffic) from the outside. In some cases, larger organizations or internet service providers may employ a technique called "subnetting," which can give portions of their network unique external IP addresses, but for home users, this is generally not the case. So, while each device on a home network has an internal address to communicate within that network, when it comes to the wider internet, they all funnel through that one external IP address.
